title: Decisions and loops
subtitle: Sequence, selection, repetition: every program ever written is built from these three.

sections.title: if, else if, else
sections.body:
Life is full of forks: if it is raining, take an umbrella; else if it is sunny, wear sunglasses; else do nothing. A program needs exactly the same thing, and if (cond) { … } else if (cond2) { … } else { … } is how you say it. The conditions are tried in order, and only the first true branch runs, like a grade ladder you climb from the top.

Two traps wait for you here. First, = assigns while == compares, and mixing them up inside a condition is a legend among bugs. Second, the “dangling else”: an else belongs to the nearest if, so use braces and spare yourself the confusion. What do you think if (x = 5) actually does? Keep that question in mind.

choices.text: Assigns 5 to x and is always true.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1.1 — grade ladder

keynotes: Only the first true branch of an if / else if / else chain runs, and conditions are tried in order.
An else belongs to the nearest if, so use braces to avoid the dangling else.

sections.title: switch
sections.body:
When you have many choices based on one value, a long ladder of ifs gets tiresome. switch (n) { case 1: …; break; case 2: …; break; default: … } jumps straight to the matching case. Watch the figure: it lands directly on case 3.

Here is the catch that bites everyone once. Without break, control falls through to the next case. Sometimes that is exactly what you want; far more often it is a bug. One more rule: the selector must be an integer or char.

figures.caption: Figure 5.2.1 — switch

keynotes: switch jumps to the matching case; default catches the rest.
Without break control falls through to the next case, sometimes useful, often a bug.
The selector must be an integer or char.

sections.title: for loop
sections.body:
Now for repetition, the thing computers are truly good at. If you know how many times to repeat, reach for the for loop: for (init; condition; update) body. Three parts, one order: init once, test before each pass, update after each pass.

Let’s count passes. For for (i = 0; i < n; i++) with n = 10, i takes 0, 1, …, 9, which is ten passes. Notice it is ten, not eleven; the loop stops the moment i reaches 10. The classic question is whether you can spot that off-by-one before it bites. Step through the figure to watch the sum of even numbers 1–10 grow (2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10) only when i is even.

worked.why: Iterations of for (i = 0; i < n; i++) when n = 10.

questions.prompt: How many times does for (i = 1; i <= 5; i++) run its body?

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Off by one the other way.

figures.caption: Figure 5.3.1 — for loop
figures.note: Step through: watch sum grow only on even i.

problems.prompt: What does the program above print if the condition is changed to i % 3 == 0?

keynotes: for (init; condition; update) runs init once, tests before each pass and updates after each pass.
Use it when the number of repetitions is known.
With n = 10, i takes 0 to 9: ten passes.

sections.title: while and do–while
sections.body:
What if you do not know in advance how many times to repeat? You keep going until something happens, like stirring until the sugar dissolves. That is while (cond). It tests first, so it may run zero times. Its sibling do { … } while (cond); runs the body first, so it always runs at least once.

Two helpers sit inside any loop: break leaves the loop entirely, and continue skips to the next pass. In the figure, 5! = 120 is computed with a while loop, and the do–while counts down.

questions.prompt: A do–while body runs at least…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The test is at the bottom.

figures.caption: Figure 5.4.1 — while and do–while

keynotes: while tests first so it may run zero times; do–while runs at least once.
Use while when the count is unknown.
break leaves a loop; continue skips to the next pass.

sections.title: Nested loops and patterns
sections.body:
Now put a loop inside a loop, like the hands of a clock: the minute hand goes round for each step of the hour hand. An outer loop of m passes containing an inner loop of n passes runs the inner body m × n times. That is how tables, matrices and patterns are made, and it is also where the O(n²) cost comes from.

Try the triangle of stars, where row i prints i stars. With 4 rows the inner body runs 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 times, which is 4·5/2 = 10. Can you see the shortcut for adding 1 to n? Remember it, because you will use it again when we count the cost of algorithms.

worked.why: Outer 4 passes, inner up to row number: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4.

questions.prompt: Outer loop 6 passes, inner 7 passes. Inner body runs…

keynotes: An outer loop of m passes with an inner loop of n passes runs the inner body m × n times.
Nested loops build tables, matrices and patterns, and give O(n²) cost.
A 4-row triangle of stars runs the inner body 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 times.

sections.title: Choosing the right loop
sections.body:
Which loop should you pick? Ask yourself one question: what do I know about the repetition? Here is the answer in a table you can come back to.

NeedUse
Known countfor
Repeat until a condition, maybe zero timeswhile
Run once, then repeat whiledo–while
Choose among constantsswitch

Think of a menu that must appear at least once and repeat until the user quits. Which row does that match? You have the answer already.

questions.prompt: Menu shown at least once, repeated until the user quits:

keynotes: Use for when the count is known, while when it may run zero times, and do–while when it must run at least once.
Use switch to choose among constants.
A menu shown at least once and repeated until the user quits is a do–while.
